name: tdlib-p17
build_steps: test -d ta/stx || (rm -rf stx-btree && git init -q stx-btree && git -C stx-btree fetch -q --depth 1 https://github.com/bingmann/stx-btree.git eff5e36975b62327755b2e05fd19c882ea6b4b0c && git -C stx-btree checkout -q FETCH_HEAD && mkdir -p ta && cp -r stx-btree/include/stx ta/ && rm -rf stx-btree)
grep -q 'static unsigned dummy' tdlib/src/graph_traits.hpp || sed -i 's/unsigned dummy;/static unsigned dummy;/' tdlib/src/graph_traits.hpp

grep -q 'inline unsigned bagsize_t::dummy' tdlib/src/graph_traits.hpp || sed -i '0,/^} \/\/ treedec/s/^} \/\/ treedec/inline unsigned bagsize_t::dummy = 0;\n} \/\/ treedec/' tdlib/src/graph_traits.hpp
description: TDLIB PACE 2017 submission (C++ port of Tamaki + heuristic)
notes: tw-exact and tw-heuristic are both 'grtd -m <mask>' wrappers; -m is a bitmask selecting the algorithm threads (tdlib/grtd/grtd.cc): 64 = USE_TA, the Tamaki exact algorithm; 128 = USE_P17, the PACE 2017 heuristics. So the exact/heuristic switch is real, not a parameter tweak. The top-level Makefile skips any stage whose *-stamp file exists, so a rebuild would keep a stale grtd (e.g. one linked against a Boost version that has since been removed); the stamps and build/ are deleted before make so every setup run configures and links afresh. configure forces -std=c++11, under which exact.hpp's passing of a variadic config template to a template template parameter with one parameter is rejected (by g++ 12 and 15 alike; clang 20 fails elsewhere); -fnew-ttp-matching applies the C++17 P0522 matching rule while keeping C++11 (with -std=gnu++17 instead, GCC 15 rejects gala's templates under -Wtemplate-body). Known upstream defects: in heuristic mode, when preprocessing reduces the whole graph (trees, BarbellGraph_10_5, pace2017 ex004), the P17 thread commits an upper bound of bagsize 1 computed on the empty kernel, so the 's td' header claims width 0 over correct bags (grtd itself prints 'c bug? 1 <real bagsize>'); the runner's header check records these as invalid, with or without --validate. In exact mode TA can stop with 'memory exhausted: 52428800' and exit 1 (ex003), which the runner records as an error.

name: arboretum

notes: Cargo.lock pins num-bigint 0.4.0, which no longer compiles with current rustc; the first step bumps it to 0.4.3 (semver-compatible). The handle-ctrlc feature makes the heuristic print its best decomposition on SIGTERM; -t makes it stop by itself before the runner's deadline. The exact command ignores both and runs to completion.

name: goatd

notes: Needs Rust 1.88+ (edition 2024) and a C++20 compiler (g++ 12+ or clang) for the vendored FlowCutter. The soft budget is half the internal limit and the hard budget the whole of it, in milliseconds, so the portfolio's final stages finish before the runner's deadline; it also prints its best decomposition on SIGTERM.

name: cliquetrees-jl
description: CliqueTrees.jl: PIDBT exact algorithm with safe rules/separators, min-fill heuristic (Julia)
notes: The wrapper (config/cliquetrees_wrapper.jl) parses the .gr file, runs SafeRules(SafeSeparators(PIDBT())) or MF() and writes a .td; a forest from a disconnected graph is chained into one tree. As with treewidth-solver-jl, every run pays Julia's package load and compile time (10-15 s).

name: libtw
authors: Thomas van Dijk, Jan-Pieter van den Heuvel, Wouter Slob
description: LibTW (treewidth.com, 2006): subset dynamic programming exact algorithm, greedy fill-in heuristic (Java)
notes: LibTW is a library without a PACE front end, so config/LibtwRunner.java reads the .gr file and prints 'c width <w>' (no bags, so --validate cannot check it). Exact mode runs TreewidthDP seeded with the greedy fill-in bound; it holds every subset of vertices and only finishes on small graphs. 'quickbb' selects LibTW's Java port of QuickBB instead. The GitHub mirror is the treewidth.com release with small fixes.

name: triangulator
description: Triangulator: Bouchitte-Todinca algorithm over enumerated potential maximal cliques (C++)
notes: Exact Bouchitte-Todinca dynamic programming over all potential maximal cliques, listed with the Bouchitte-Todinca enumeration; the same code base placed second in the PACE 2017 minimum fill-in track. -treewidth reads a PACE .gr from stdin and writes the decomposition ('s td' header, bags, tree edges) to stdout; the optimal width, fill edge count and time go to stderr. Disconnected and edgeless graphs come out as a single tree. Builds with the top-level Makefile (plain C++11, no extra libraries). The author notes that Laakeri/triangulator-msc is faster, but that build links CPLEX and MaxHS unconditionally, so this version is used.

name: triangulator-msc
description: Triangulator (2020 master's thesis version): Bouchitte-Todinca algorithm with preprocessing and a faster potential maximal clique enumerator (C++)
notes: The successor of triangulator, which the author reports it outperforms. Upstream links CPLEX and MaxHS unconditionally and, in tw mode, prints only 'Treewidth: <w>' to stderr without the decomposition. config/triangulator-msc-no-cplex.patch removes the CPLEX/MaxHS objects (ghtw, ftw, hypercost, maxhs_iface, the CharRemoveMaxSat and BuildColorMaxSAT functions) from the Makefile and sources, and adds a PACE .td writer to main.cpp: bags are the vertices of a perfect elimination order of the returned chordal graph with their later neighbours, and the parent of a bag is the bag of the earliest later neighbour. The patch also reads stdin before parsing so that comment lines (which the upstream reader would take as edges when they have two tokens), blank lines (which trip an assert) and self-loops (another assert) are dropped, and so that isolated vertices, which the upstream reader never sees, get bags of their own from the header's vertex count. Logging is left at upstream's default, so stderr carries a few progress lines per run. Built with -march=native, so the binary is tied to the machine it was built on.

name: treedec
build_steps: test -f gala/graph.h || (rm -rf gala && git init -q gala && git -C gala fetch -q --depth 1 https://github.com/freetdi/gala.git 875bd2a939cce6c32768369b1383752ec5aab77d && git -C gala checkout -q FETCH_HEAD)
mkdir -p build && cd build && ../configure --without-python CPPFLAGS="-DNDEBUG -I$PWD/.." CXXFLAGS="-g -O2 -fpermissive"
description: treedec (tdlib) library driver tdecomp: --ex17 preprocessing + Tamaki exact, --ppfitm preprocessing + fill-in + triangulation minimisation heuristic (C++)
notes: The library behind tdlib-p17, at its 2025 head, driven through its example program examples/tdecomp, which reads a .gr on stdin and writes a .td. tdecomp is built only when configure finds the gala headers (freetdi/gala, GPL-3.0, header-only), so the first step clones gala at a pinned commit into the solver directory and configure gets -I for it; the fourth step fails loudly if configure still did not pick it up, since make would otherwise silently build nothing. Only the tdecomp target is built, together with the 'treedec' target of examples/Makefile.am, a symlink to src/ that <treedec/...> includes resolve through; 'make all' would create it as a built source, 'make tdecomp' alone does not. GCC 15 rejects two uninstantiated template bodies in src/tr_bag.h (-Wtemplate-body); -fpermissive turns them into warnings and is understood by older GCCs too, unlike -Wno-template-body. gala's incomplete() macro prints 'incomplete <file>:<line>' to stdout from fill_in_edges on every run, which the .td validator rejects as a malformed line; both gala's and treedec's definitions are guarded by #ifndef, so defining it as (void)0 on the command line silences it. The define is passed to make, not to configure: configure splits CPPFLAGS on whitespace without quote removal, so the parentheses reach the compiler with literal quotes and the 'C compiler works' check fails. tdecomp's reader takes every non-comment line as an edge and crashes on a blank line, and its gala graph has no self-loops, so 'u u' crashes it too; the runner therefore feeds it a simple-graph copy (input_format pace_gr_simple: comments, blank lines, self-loops and parallel edges dropped, edge count rewritten). Algorithm flags measured on named graphs: --ppfitm matched or beat --fi, --fitm, --bmd, --ppmd and --thorup everywhere, so it is the heuristic; --ex17 is preprocessing plus Tamaki's PID algorithm, i.e. the PACE 2017 exact entry rebuilt from the current library (tdlib-p17 runs the frozen 2017 submission). Other flags exist (--ta, --tr, --fi, --ppfi, --fitm, --bmd, --ppmd, --thorup, --pp); --he17 is compiled out and prints no decomposition. The heuristics finish on their own in well under a second; on SIGTERM the exact mode exits without a decomposition, which the runner records as a timeout. Single-threaded. examples/Makefile.am adds -march=native, so the binary is tied to the machine it was built on.

name: passagemath
build_steps: python3 -c 'import sys; sys.exit("passagemath needs Python 3.11 or newer" if sys.version_info < (3, 11) else 0)'
description: SageMath's exact treewidth, Graph.treewidth(algorithm='sage'), via the pip-installable passagemath-graphs (Python/Cython)
notes: passagemath ships parts of the Sage library as pip wheels, so there is no repository to clone: the solver directory only holds a venv (about 430 MB, 108 MB downloaded) and the wrapper config/passagemath_wrapper.py. Every package is pinned by config/passagemath-constraints.txt; the venv is recreated on each setup run (pip's cache makes that quick). The cliquer extra is required, because treewidth() calls clique_number(), which imports sage.graphs.cliquer and fails without it. memory_allocator has no wheel and is compiled from its sdist, which needs gcc and the Python headers (python3-dev). The 'sage' algorithm decides treewidth <= k for increasing k by dynamic programming over pairs of a cut of at most k+1 vertices and a component of the rest; it is named explicitly because the default switches to tdlib when passagemath-tdlib is present, and tdlib is what tdlib-p17 and treedec already run. It is far slower than the PACE solvers (BrinkmannGraph 50 s and CoxeterGraph 119 s, where tamaki-2017 needs 0.3 s), but finishes small graphs instantly; Python start-up and the Sage import add about 0.3 s per run. The wrapper parses the .gr itself (comments, blank lines, self-loops and parallel edges are dropped; isolated vertices kept) and stops on SIGTERM without output, which the runner records as a timeout. The last build step runs the wrapper on tests/k4.gr, so an install that imports but cannot compute fails the build instead of every run.

name: halin-tw
description: Halin graphs only: Eppstein's linear-time recognition, then the linear-time H-Td algorithm of Alejandro-Soto, Trejo-Sanchez and Segura for a width-3 decomposition (C++17)
notes: An implementation, written from the papers rather than from the authors' code (none is published), of H-Td (Alejandro-Soto, Trejo-Sanchez, Segura, arXiv:2506.02346, 2025) on top of Eppstein's reduction-based Halin recognition (JGAA 20(2), 2016). Both steps are linear-time. bin/halin_td reads a .gr on stdin and either writes a width-3 .td to stdout or, for any graph that is not Halin, prints 'error: input is not a Halin graph (<reason>)' to stderr and exits 2; not_applicable_exit_code turns that into status not_applicable, while exit 1 (unreadable input) stays an error. Every Halin graph has treewidth exactly 3, so an ok row always says 3; the bags are not deduplicated across tree nodes (K4 gives 7 bags, three of them equal), which is still a valid decomposition. The recognizer rejects self-loops and parallel edges as non-Halin, so the runner feeds it a simple-graph copy (input_format pace_gr_simple). Only bin/halin_td is built; the repository's Makefile also builds a generator, a validator and a brute-force test that the runner does not use. Plain C++17 with -O2, no libraries. On all eight benchmark sets (6036 instances, 60 s, --validate) it accepted exactly 9 (named-graphs FruchtGraph, TetrahedralGraph, WheelGraph_100; pace2016-testbed WheelGraph_100; five 5-vertex wheels among the transit graphs), all valid with width 3 and matching tamaki-2017; it declined the other 6027, with no errors and no run over 3 s (the road graphs included). An independent networkx check (a face F of the planar embedding such that G - E(F) is a tree without degree-2 vertices whose leaves are exactly V(F)) picks out the same 9 instances. On random Halin graphs from the repository's gen_halin, a 238,000-vertex graph takes 0.48 s through the runner, while tamaki-2017 already times out at 30 s on 7,500 vertices.

name: bfk-treewidth-2approx
description: The optimized 2-approximation of Belbasi, Fürer and Kumar: a min-degree decomposition rebuilt by dynamic programming over a grouped tree decomposition until its width is at most 2*tw+1 (C++17)
notes: An implementation, written by Claude Opus 5.5 from the paper, of M. Belbasi, M. Fürer, M. Kumar, Optimized 2-Approximation of Treewidth (arXiv:2411.16918v3). Only bin/tw2approx is built (make bin/tw2approx; the Makefile compiles with -O2 -march=native -std=c++17 and needs no libraries); the repository's generator and verifier are not used. It reads the .gr on stdin and accepts comments, blank lines, self-loops and parallel edges, but, like the runner's own reader, requires exactly m edge lines, so it gets the instance unchanged. In its default (auto) mode it builds a min-degree elimination decomposition and takes the degeneracy as a lower bound lb; while the width cw exceeds 2*lb+1 it applies the paper's Theorem 1 with k = max(lb, floor(cw/4)), which either rebuilds the decomposition with width <= 2k+1 or proves tw > k and raises lb to k+1. An answer therefore always has width <= 2*tw+1. The first stdout line, 'c width W, k K, tw lower bound L', also gives the lower bound, which the runner does not record. Every node keeps a DP table of L^|bag| int32 entries (L = 3 or 4), so only graphs with a narrow min-degree decomposition get past the table-memory guard (--mem-gb, default 24 GB); the upstream README puts the limit at a width of about 16, and on the benchmarks the widest min-degree decomposition improved had width 14 while every exit 3 outside the road graphs had width 14 or more. When the tables would exceed the guard, the program prints 'error: component C: memory limit: ...' and exits 3, which the runner records as 'error: exit 3'. For most instances that happens before any DP (1078 of the 1242 exit-3 runs outside the road graphs ended within 1 s), but it can also come at a larger k, after rounds that proved tw > k. A run can approach the full 24 GB, so allow that much per job with --jobs. There is no SIGTERM handler, so a timeout leaves no answer. On all eight benchmark sets (6036 instances, 60 s, --validate): 4636 ok, all valid; 1252 error: exit 3; 148 timeout; no invalid, parse_error or other error; peak memory 22.9 GB (PSS). Only 30 of the ok results are narrower than the min-degree decomposition; the other 4606 are that decomposition itself, already within the bound because its width is at most 2*degeneracy+1. The road graphs all end in exit 3 or a timeout. Checked against tamaki-2017 (30 s) on the 470 instances, other than the empty graph, that finished in a 10 s scan, leaving out the control-flow graphs and the transit graphs whose min-degree width was not improved: tamaki-2017 solved 415, and on all 415 the width is at most 2*tw+1 and the lower bound at most tw; the width equals tw on 277. The empty graph gives 's td 0 0 0', recorded as width -1.

name: tamaki-treewidth-sea2019
description: Reimplementation of Tamaki's SEA 2019 algorithm from the talk slides: msDP over exact and heuristic lists of minimal separators, with the ascending and descending searches alternated (C++20)
notes: An implementation, written by Claude Opus 5.5, of H. Tamaki, Computing treewidth via exact and heuristic lists of minimal separators (SEA 2019), reconstructed from the talk slides (Shonan Meeting 144, March 2019) because the paper itself was not available; it is not Tamaki's code, and shares nothing with tamaki-2016 or tamaki-2017 but the author of the algorithm. The upstream README lists where it had to guess or deviate from the slides; every change keeps a YES answer a valid decomposition. msDP(G, k, Delta) decides tw <= k by dynamic programming over connected sets whose neighbourhoods lie in a list Delta of minimal separators, without enumerating potential maximal cliques; listExact(G, k) lists every minimal separator of size <= k, and listHeuristic grows a list from the bags of a min-fill decomposition. -m alternate interleaves the ascending search (k up from the MMD+ lower bound, exact lists) with the descending one (the min-fill upper bound improved with growing heuristic lists), keeping their running times equal. It is used instead of the default -m ascend: on named-graphs (30 s, 4 jobs) ascend solved 111 and alternate 113, with the same widths (tamaki-2017: 112), and the upstream README reports 162 against 171 of the 200 PACE 2017 exact-track instances in 30 s. Safe reductions (simplicial and almost simplicial vertices) are on by default, and each connected component is solved separately. Only tw is built (make tw: -std=c++20 -O2 -march=native, no libraries, so the binary is tied to the machine it was built on); td-validate and the tests are not. It reads the .gr on stdin, skips comments and blank lines, ignores self-loops and merges parallel edges, but, like the runner's reader, requires exactly m edge lines, so it gets the instance unchanged. Single-threaded and without a SIGTERM handler, so a timeout leaves no answer. The empty graph gives 's td 0 0 0', recorded as width -1. Memory: each vertex keeps its neighbourhood as an n-bit set, so the adjacency alone takes n^2/8 bytes (1.25 GB at 100,000 vertices, 5 GB at 200,000, 125 GB at 1,000,000), allocated as the graph is read, and nothing bounds it. The largest PACE 2017 heuristic-track graphs (up to 15.5 million vertices) and the road graphs (264,346 to 24.6 million) are far beyond that, so with --jobs they can exhaust memory: in a first attempt with 8 jobs and only a 44 GB limit on the whole run, he171 (373,241 vertices) had reached 10 GB after 19 s when it was killed. The figures below were therefore measured with each process under ulimit -v 5 GiB (8 jobs, so at most 40 GiB). A run that reaches the limit while reading prints 'input error: std::bad_alloc' and exits 1; one that reaches it while solving aborts, which the runner sees as exit 134 from the shell. On all eight benchmark sets (6036 instances, 60 s, --validate, 8 jobs): 4795 ok, all valid; 1201 timeout; 40 errors, all at the 5 GiB limit and all on graphs with 154,188 or more vertices (26 PACE 2017 heuristic-track instances, the 13 road graphs and EUR in pace2016-testbed). The largest solved graph has 10,200 vertices, and no ok run was seen above 141 MB (PSS, sampled every 100 ms). With the limit raised to 20 GiB (2 jobs), the 11 of the 40 with at most 310,000 vertices still did not finish: 10 timed out and he173 reached 20 GiB as well. Of the 200 PACE 2017 exact-track instances it solved 173 (162 within 30 s). Checked against tamaki-2017 (60 s, 7 jobs, heap capped at 5 GB with JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-Xmx5g; 10 of its 1415 timeouts came near that cap) on the other 5996 instances: both solved 4560, with the same width on every one; only tamaki-treewidth-sea2019 solved 235 (155 transit graphs, 33 PACE 2017, 26 PACE 2017 bonus, 16 PACE 2016, 4 named, 1 UAI) and only tamaki-2017 21 (19 PACE 2017, 1 named, 1 UAI). triangulator-msc (60 s, 8 jobs, ulimit -v 5 GiB) solved 17 of those 235, with the same widths; the widths of the other 218 have not been confirmed by a second exact solver (their decompositions are valid, so each is at least an upper bound).

name: jdrasil-approx
authors: Max Bannach, Sebastian Berndt, Thorsten Ehlers
description: Jdrasil's approximation mode: reduction rules and safe-separator splitting, then the Robertson-Seymour FPT approximation (width at most 4k+4) on each atom (Java)
notes: Runs jdrasil.Approximation from the same pinned commit as jdrasil, in a clone of its own so that jdrasil stays unpatched. After Jdrasil's reduction rules, GraphSplitter splits the graph along safe separators, and RobertsonSeymourDecomposer decomposes each atom: it tries k = 1, 2, ... (skipping every k with m > k*n) and returns the first decomposition it finds, whose bags have at most 4k+5 vertices. Upstream answered an exception on an atom with one bag holding the whole atom, a valid decomposition of width |atom|-1 that the runner would record as ok, and answered any other exception by printing 'c ...' on stdout and exiting 0 (recorded as parse_error). config/jdrasil-approx-fail-loudly.patch makes both exit 1 with the reason on stderr and nothing on stdout, and catches StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError the same way; forcing the decomposer to throw on PetersenGraph, upstream printed 's td 1 10 10' and exited 0, the patched build exits 1. The bound 4k+4 holds for the k the search stops at, which is at most tw only if every k it gave up on was a real obstacle. The decomposer lets the separator of S_A and S_B contain vertices of S (setDisjointToS(false)) and gives up on k when the separator lies inside S (S.equals(newS)), which the textbook algorithm does not; the patch leaves this as upstream wrote it. A probe on 28 named graphs found no such case: all 10 times it gave up on a k, no separator existed. Run with -s 42: Jdrasil's random source is unseeded by default, and the minor-min-width lower bound that sets the splitter's threshold uses it, so without a seed one graph gave width 7 in four runs and 8 in one. Fed pace_gr_simple: with the self-loop of fredericton-transit_20130313_1626 left in, both this build and the unpatched jar printed a decomposition whose tree is disconnected. There is no SIGTERM handler, so a timeout leaves no answer.

name: flowcutter-kahip
build_steps: test -f kahip/interface/kaHIP_interface.h || (rm -rf kahip && git init -q kahip && git -C kahip fetch -q --depth 1 https://github.com/KaHIP/KaHIP.git 2e86d3da2065bcf6ddbf6fb84d2b52f33db1061f && git -C kahip checkout -q FETCH_HEAD)
authors: Michael Hamann, Ben Strasser (FlowCutter code); Peter Sanders, Christian Schulz et al. (KaHIP)
description: Experimental FlowCutter code built with KaHIP: FlowCutter's CCH preprocessing, then nested dissection with KaHIP's node separator, turned into a tree decomposition (C++)
notes: kit-algo/flow-cutter is the experimental code from the development of FlowCutter (Hamann and Strasser, ALENEX 2016), not a PACE submission; its README says it was never meant for release and likely contains bugs. The run loads the graph, sorts the arcs (the KaHIP commands require sorted tails), computes a nested dissection order with reorder_nodes_in_kahip2_cch_order 0.03, and prints the tree decomposition of that elimination order. The order first handles components, puts the largest biconnected component last and degree-two chains first, and then splits the rest recursively with KaHIP's node_separator (mode STRONG, seed 42, imbalance 3%). On named-graphs (20 s per run, sequential) this variant gave a total excess over the exact width of 107 on the 111 graphs all variants solved, against 114 with imbalance 0.2 and 278 for reorder_nodes_in_kahip_cch_order, whose separator is derived from a kaffpa edge cut; the edge-cut variant is about 15 times faster (median 0.07 s against 1.2 s). Single-threaded and deterministic, with no time limit of its own and no SIGTERM output, so a timeout leaves no answer. KaHIP v3.25 (commit 2e86d3d, MIT) is cloned into kahip/ by the build and only its kahip_static target is built, with -DNOMPI=On -DPARHIP=Off (MPI is needed only by ParHIP and kaffpaE) and upstream's -march=native, so the binary is tied to the machine it was built on. When KaHIP's CMake finds METIS and GKlib it compiles them into the interface, so the link line adds the libraries recorded in kahip/build/CMakeCache.txt; this machine has no METIS, so that path is untested. flow-cutter's build.py is not used, because it compiles every .cpp below the directory, KaHIP's included; the top-level sources are compiled directly with -DNO_GPL (no readline) and -DUSE_KAHIP against KaHIP's own interface header (kahip_idx is 32-bit by default, matching flow-cutter's int*). config/flowcutter-kahip.patch changes console.cpp in four places: (1) print_pace_tree_decomposition passed the reordered graph together with the inverse of node_original_position, so it eliminated the nodes in input order and printed positions as node IDs; every reorder gave an invalid decomposition (checked on four named graphs with each order), and the patch passes the graph in input IDs with node_original_position; (2) load_pace_graph used the cached loader, which leaves a binary copy of every input, named after its path, in $CACHETMPDIR, $TMPDIR or /tmp and never deletes it, one file per run with the runner's per-run temporary paths; the patch reads the file directly; (3) print_pace_tree_decomposition threw on graphs with fewer than two nodes (15 benchmark instances); the patch prints 's td 0 0 0', or 's td 1 1 1' and 'b 1 1', as tamaki-2017 does; (4) main returned 0 after an exception, so a failure looked like missing output (parse_error); it now returns 1. Fed pace_gr_simple because the KaHIP commands reject multi-arcs and loops.
